part1-import-rules.desc: Verifies that a file's imports only point: - Sideways (to siblings in its own module); or - Deeper (into nested modules) And that they never point (violations): - Up to a parent module, unless to a commons module (see commons-modules section below); or - Across into a different branch of the tree
part1-import-rules.rationale: To keep a predictable module tree structure, where we know everything in a module's submodules are supporting logic for the module to call, and not the other way around (i.e. where submodules call up to their parent modules for supporting logic).

more-details.detail: Sideways/deeper imports must be written with `super::...` (i.e. never `crate::...`).
Imports to a commons parent module must be written with `crate::...` (i.e. never `super::super...`).
more-details.rationale: To make the code more readable by distinguishing between a sideways/deeper import and an import up to a commons parent.

commons-modules.desc: These are modules for shared code. The following are their names and what they are for: - c: free-functions - t: types - s: `static` items - cnst: `const` items - ext_traits: extension trait definition and implementations Each may be a folder (e.g. `t/`) with a mod.rs file, or a single-file module (e.g. `t.rs`)
commons-modules.examples: - `crate::c` is the whole-crate shared free-functions, reachable everywhere - `crate::app::c` is app-local, reachable only from files at or below `crate::app`
commons-modules.note: Inside a commons folder, the imports must still be sideways or deeper (i.e. `c/foo/bar.rs` cannot import `c/util.rs`, which sits above it, just because they are both in `c/`). A commons folder re-roots the tree: inside it, the same up/across prohibitions apply, but measured from the commons folder rather than the crate.
commons-modules.rationale: There must be a way to share certain items between separate modules that have different submodules, because otherwise it would be impossible to write DRY code. In fact, this might be exaggerating it, but it would maybe even be impossible to write code at all. So, if we didn't have these commons modules, the import rules would be too strict to work.

config.item: ignore_export_macros - when true, imports of `#[macro_export]` macros are exempt (default false)
